name: Thoracic extension over foam roller

card.summary: A mobility drill that arches the upper back over a foam roller, used to counter rounded posture; no trials of the drill itself were found.
card.aka: Foam roller thoracic mobilization, upper back extension
card.note: Related literature covers thoracic manipulation and sitting posture, not this specific drill.

quick.overview:
The drill involves lying with a foam roller under the upper back and extending the thoracic spine over it. It is discussed in posture routines aimed at rounded upper back and forward head carriage.
No clinical study of the foam-roller drill was located. Related research examines thoracic manipulation for neck pain and the muscle activity in different sitting postures.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say it mobilizes stiff thoracic joints so the upper back can extend and the shoulders and head sit further back. This is a proposed mechanism not demonstrated by trials of the drill.
quick.risks: No harms are documented; people with spinal conditions are generally referred to clinicians for exercise advice.

lead: Thoracic extension over a foam roller is a mobility drill in which a person lies back with a foam roller under the upper back and arches the thoracic spine over it. People use it in posture routines to loosen a stiff, rounded upper back so the chest opens, the shoulders sit further back and the head can stack over the torso.[1][2]

The looks payoff is a more upright frame. Forward head posture is described as an excessively kyphotic thoracic spine with the head forward of the shoulders, putting the ear ahead of the shoulder line and pushing the chin forward, and Wikipedia notes the upper-back joints can stiffen in flexion over time.[1] Mobilizing that region is meant to make standing tall easier to hold.

No trial has tested the foam-roller drill itself. Related research includes thoracic manipulation trials for neck pain, studies of sitting posture and trunk muscle activation, and reviews of foam rolling for short-term range of motion.[1][3][4][5]

chain: Arch upper back over a foam roller
Chest opens and shoulders and head sit back
angle.text: People use the drill to restore upper-back extension so they can stand with the shoulders back and head over the torso. Better-aligned posture reads as a broader chest and a taller, more confident frame.

No trial of the drill itself; foam-rolling reviews report short-term range-of-motion gains[5]

paras: The drill places the roller across the upper back, typically below the shoulder blades, with the person supported by the hands behind the head while extending backward over the roller. It is one of several mobility and posture exercises aimed at the thoracic spine.[2]
Postural thoracic kyphosis, according to Wikipedia, is usually linked to slouching in younger people and can often be addressed with posture re-education and strengthening exercises.[2]

Kyphosis is an abnormally excessive convex curvature of the spine. Postural kyphosis is the most common type, usually results from slouching, can occur at any age and is often reversible with muscle correction, whereas Scheuermann's kyphosis is a rigid structural form seen mostly in teenagers in which the person cannot consciously correct their posture.[2] Wikipedia gives a normal thoracic angle of about 20 to 45 degrees measured by the Cobb method, with larger curves classed as hyperkyphosis.[2]

Forward head posture is described as one of the most common postural problems and is linked to prolonged hunching over laptops, tablets and phones and to occupations with sustained bent postures. Wikipedia describes thoracic joints stiffening in the flexed position while mid-back support muscles weaken and the deep neck flexors lose strength, and says a stiff thoracic segment may need hands-on mobilisation because exercise tends to move already-mobile segments more.[1]
Treatment of postural kyphosis in the Wikipedia kyphosis article centres on posture retraining and strengthening exercises, with bracing and surgery reserved for structural or severe cases.[2]

The thoracic spine consists of twelve vertebrae, T1 to T12, between the cervical and lumbar regions, and the ribs attach to T1 through T10 by facets on the transverse processes as well as to the vertebral bodies.[6] Wikipedia's anatomy page does not describe extension range, so the drill's effect on segmental motion is described in practitioner terms rather than anatomical measurement here.[6]

A foam roller is a cylinder of elastomeric foam used for self-massage, classified as self-myofascial release. Rollers vary in size and firmness, with soft rollers recommended for beginners.[5] People use them to improve flexibility, reduce soreness and ease muscle knots.[5]

Two reviews cited by Wikipedia found that rolling gives a short-term improvement in joint range of motion, with long-term benefits unknown, and that combining rolling with stretching gives no significant extra gain over either alone. A meta-analysis suggested rolling is better justified as a warm-up than as a recovery tool but found that rolling after exercise reduced perceived muscle pain.[5] These findings concern rolling of muscles, not the extension drill over the roller described here.

Forward head posture is described as an excessively kyphotic thoracic spine and, combined with rounded shoulders, is called upper crossed syndrome. Wikipedia lists strengthening the mid and lower back, shoulder-blade retractors and deep neck flexors, and stretching tight muscles, as common exercise approaches, and describes thoracic mobilization as a way to free stiff upper-back joints.[1]
Proponents use the foam-roller version at home as a mobility step before strengthening work, with the aim of improving the visible alignment of head, shoulders and spine.
In looksmaxxing and posture communities the drill is typically described alongside wall angels, rows and chin tucks as part of a routine to undo desk posture.

sections.h: Use in lifting and training routines
paras: Outside posture-specific programs, thoracic extension appears as a warm-up or between-set movement in strength training logs on T Nation. One lifter lists an overhead thoracic extension in a 10-minute mobility flow before jerks and push presses; another uses a kneeling thoracic extension and twist stretch between rounds of rows and shrugs; a third includes thoracic extension in a recovery-day mobility block.[7][8][9]

Coaches in those threads also use the term for rib and spine position under the bar. One poster describes the 'ribs down' cue used in powerlifting squats as the opposite of the thoracic extension position used by Olympic lifters in high-bar squats, and another describes ribs flared or tucked as thoracic extension or flexion in a bracing discussion.[10][11] These uses are about lifting positions and are separate from the foam-roller drill, though they show how the term circulates in training communities.

No studies found on the foam-roller drill itself. Related work includes a 2005 randomized trial of thoracic manipulation, cited by Wikipedia, that reported immediate neck-pain reduction.[1] A 2006 Spine study compared spinal-pelvic curvature and trunk muscle activation in upright and slump sitting in pain-free people, and a 2014 case-control study examined sensorimotor tests in 30 people with recurrent neck pain and 30 controls.[3][4]

Reviews summarised for foam rolling report short-term range-of-motion gains,[5] while Wikipedia's account of forward head posture cites a 2019 systematic review that found a link between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not adolescents.[1]

lore.intro: Thoracic extension over a roller circulates in posture and mobility routines and in strength-training logs, where it is listed as a warm-up or between-set movement.[7][8]

claims.claim: Arching over a roller restores upper-back extension and improves posture
claims.believers: Posture-routine advocates say mobilising stiff thoracic joints lets the shoulders and head sit back so standing tall is easier to hold.[1]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested the foam-roller drill; Wikipedia describes thoracic mobilisation and manipulation as options for stiff segments and a trial showing immediate neck-pain reduction after thoracic manipulation.[1]

claims.believers: Users say rolling improves flexibility and eases tightness.[5]
claims.experts: Reviews cited by Wikipedia report short-term range-of-motion improvement with unknown long-term effect.[5]

claims.claim: Thoracic extension work belongs in a lifter's warm-up and helps overhead and squat positions
claims.believers: Training-log posters list thoracic extension in mobility flows before overhead lifts and between pulling sets, and coaches discuss thoracic extension as a bar-position variable.[7][8][10]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested the foam-roller drill for lifting performance or posture; the sitting-posture study of pain-free adults examined spinal curvature and trunk muscle activation, not mobility drills.[3]
